The backmost prisoner counts red hats among the 99 in front and says red if that count is odd, blue if even. This encodes the parity of the front 99 hats. That spoken color encodes the parity of the 99 hats in front. Each subsequent prisoner then uses the parity announced by those behind plus the colors of the hats he can see in front to deduce his own hat color uniquely: if the number of red hats among the hats in front he sees is t (mod 2), he computes his hat color as a = s xor t (where s is the parity encoded by the previously spoken color(s)) and announces that. Repeating this, every prisoner except the first can determine their own color with certainty. Therefore, at least 99 survivors are guaranteed (the first speaker may die, depending on his actual hat).

In a Vickrey (sealed-bid second-price) auction, the winner pays the second-highest bid. Your own bid only affects whether you win; the price you pay (if you win) is determined by others’ bids, not your bid. Therefore bidding your true value is a dominant strategy: you never pay more than your value, and you maximize your payoff by winning when the item’s value exceeds the second-highest bid. With a true value of 100, the optimal bid is 100.

Repeating this argument backward through all rounds shows that in every round, defection is the best response to the other player’s strategy. Therefore the unique subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium is that both players defect in every round (i.e., always defect in all 100 rounds). To find the probability of at least one pair in a 5-card hand, compute the complement: no pair means all five cards have distinct ranks. Count of no-pair hands = C(13,5) * 4^5 = 1287 * 1024 = 1,317,888. Total 5-card hands = C(52,5) = 2,598,960. So P(no pair) = 1,317,888 / 2,598,960 ≈ 0.5071. Therefore P(at least one pair) = 1 − P(no pair) ≈ 0.4929, which rounds to 0.493.
